alt: A train due at 8:10 arrives at 8:50, described four ways: neutral (“arrived”), indignant (“limped in... yet again, with no apology”), wry (“graciously joined us... having evidently found better things to do”) and resigned (“as it does... filed on, used to it”).
caption: Tone is traced to specific words: same facts, different attitudes.

alt: Six vague tone labels (negative, positive, serious, funny, neutral, sad) each replaced by precise words, such as scornful, indignant and bitter for negative, or wry and sardonic for funny. Below, pairs like “wry but affectionate” and a five-step method for analysing tone.
caption: “Negative” says little; “scornful and controlled” says what the attitude is.

alt: Lincoln’s closing words and Douglass’s Rochester sentence traced side by side from words to connotations to tone to purpose: Lincoln’s “charity for all” and “bind up the nation’s wounds” give a conciliatory, humble tone aimed at reconciliation; Douglass’s “sham” and “swelling vanity” give a scornful, controlled tone aimed at confronting his audience.
caption: Both address a nation’s ideals; their tones differ because their purposes differ.

after: ## Worked example 1: identifying tone from word choice
alt: The sports-hall passage with key phrases labelled: “visiting dignitary” (mock-formal), “cut a ribbon” (a routine gesture), “spoke for forty minutes” (tedium), “legacy” in quotation marks (doubted), and “Still, the buffet was excellent” (a deflating anticlimax). The tone is wry and sceptical.
caption: Mock-formal words, a quoted term and an anticlimax build a wry, sceptical tone.

alt: The neutral sentence “The caretaker repaired the roof on Tuesday” branches into a respectful version (“kindly”, “grateful”, “patient”) and a sarcastic one (“finally managed”, “only three weeks after it started to leak”).
caption: The facts stay; the words, and so the attitudes, change.
